questions.prompt: What keeps a main-sequence star from collapsing under its own gravity?
options: Nothing — stars slowly shrink throughout their lives
The outward pressure of energy released by fusion in the core
The magnetic field of the star pushing on itself
Rotation spinning the star apart
questions.explanation: Fusion in the core generates heat, which creates outward pressure. When that pressure exactly balances gravity's inward pull, the star holds a constant size — hydrostatic equilibrium.
questions.misconception: It feels natural that a crushing force means the star should shrink forever, but fusion energy constantly re-pressurizes the core, so a star in equilibrium neither grows nor shrinks for billions of years.

questions.prompt: You see two similar stars: one red-orange, one blue-white. Which is hotter at its surface?
options: The red-orange one
The blue-white one
Both always have the exact same surface temperature
Color has nothing to do with temperature
questions.explanation: Color is a thermometer. A surface at about 3,000 K glows red, at 5,800 K yellow-white, and above 10,000 K blue-white. The blue star's surface is thousands of degrees hotter.
questions.misconception: Associating red with 'hot' (like a fire) and blue with 'cold' is exactly backwards for stars: blue-white means the surface is hotter.

questions.prompt: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old. Roughly where is it in its main-sequence lifetime?
options: At the very start
About halfway — around 4.6 billion of ~10 billion years
At the very end right now
Ages don't apply to stars; the Sun never changes
questions.explanation: Sun-like stars fuse hydrogen for roughly 10 billion years. At about 4.6 billion, the Sun is a little past the halfway mark, with roughly the same time left.
questions.misconception: The Sun feels eternal, so 'halfway' sounds like a claim that a huge change is coming soon — but ~5 billion years ahead is more than Earth's whole history so far.

questions.prompt: Star A has 10 × the Sun's mass. Compared with the Sun, how long will star A stay on the main sequence?
options: About 10 × longer, because it has 10 × more fuel
Much shorter — it burns fuel so fast it lives only millions of years
Exactly the same, because balance keeps all stars equal
Forever — the extra gravity boosts fusion
questions.explanation: With 10 × the mass, the core is far hotter and fuses fuel tens of thousands of times faster (luminosity scales steeply with mass). The bigger star dies in millions of years; small red dwarfs last for hundreds of billions.
questions.misconception: The intuition 'more fuel = longer life' is sound — but the fusion rate rises sharply with mass, and the hungry core easily overtakes the extra fuel.

questions.prompt: A photon of light born at the Sun's core takes about how long to escape the Sun?
options: A few milliseconds — light is that fast
About 8 minutes total
About 8 minutes for the last stretch, after wandering inside for many thousands of years
It never escapes — the Sun only reflects light in
questions.explanation: The photon constantly bumps into charged particles and is re-emitted in random directions, so its path crawls outward for roughly 10,000 to 170,000 years. Once free at the photosphere, the light reaches Earth 8 minutes later.
questions.misconception: Light leaving a star sounds instant because light is fast — but inside the dense star it is absorbed and re-emitted constantly, turning a fast particle into a slow journey.
